title: Supreme Court Presses Centre on Steep Mark-Ups on Medicines, Devices
excerpt: Bench asks why a 30 percent trade-margin cap should cover only cancer drugs, citing a stent sold at five times its price to retailers
body:
• A Supreme Court bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta has asked why the Centre's proposed 30 percent trade-margin cap is limited to specified cancer drugs and should not extend to medicines and medical devices more widely.
  • The court cited a cardiac stent priced to retailers at Rs 5,000 with an MRP of Rs 25,000, and an earlier case of a drug supplied at about Rs 2,700 and sold at Rs 27,000.
  • The Centre argues India already has some of the lowest medicine prices in the world and warns excessive intervention could affect availability.
  • Petitioners say about 82 percent of medicines fall outside scheduled price control under the DPCO, 2013.

The Supreme Court has called for a broader examination of drug pricing in India, questioning why the Centre's proposed trade-margin regulation is limited to cancer medicines and urging it to consider steep mark-ups across medicines and medical devices.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta took note of the Centre's decision to impose a 30 percent cap on trade margins for specified cancer drugs, but asked why similar scrutiny could not extend further. "This relates to only cancer drugs. What about the overall?" the bench asked. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the court the government would notify a list of cancer drugs covered by the cap, to be updated periodically, excluding inexpensive drugs.

The gaps the court put to the government

The bench cited the distance between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP), referring to an Indian-made cardiac stent with a PTR of Rs 5,000 and an MRP of Rs 25,000, and observed, "A drip line for saline, MRP is Rs 11, and it is selling for Rs 270." It also raised the pricing of azithromycin and asked the government to explain how such pricing served patients.

"If you put a cap of 16 percent, you will reduce (medical) interventions by three-fourths. Doctors cause interventions to be done because the margins are so high," the bench remarked, referring to the 16 percent retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013. The Solicitor General responded that cardiac stents were already subject to price caps.

The latest hearing follows earlier sittings in which the court used stronger language. On September 29, the bench described the mark-up on a cancer drug supplied to retailers for around Rs 3,000 and sold for Rs 27,000 as "carnage", and asked why the 16 percent margin should not apply uniformly. At an earlier hearing it had called the gap between PTR and MRP "dacoity" and "extortion", observing that people sell houses and ornaments to pay for treatment. The court has also pointed out that when treatment is funded under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, inflated prices are ultimately borne by taxpayers.

What the petitions seek

The court is hearing petitions by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking regulation of drug, medical equipment and generic medicine prices, including initial prices of non-scheduled medicines, caps on medical devices and mandatory generic prescriptions.

Jain has submitted that around 82 percent of medicines fall outside the scheduled category under the DPCO, 2013, and are therefore not subject to ceiling prices, allowing manufacturers greater freedom in fixing MRPs, subject to annual increase limits.

At the September hearing, the Solicitor General said private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, benefited from steep mark-ups. The bench also flagged hospitals requiring patients to buy from in-house pharmacies, leaving little choice to buy the same drugs more cheaply elsewhere.

The government's response

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati submitted that drug price regulation must balance affordability, availability and market considerations, and that the government could not regulate the entire pharmaceutical ecosystem. "We don't want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs," she said. Bhati said India already had some of the lowest medicine prices globally and cautioned that excessive intervention could disrupt market dynamics and affect availability. The government has also argued in the proceedings that areas with lower sales, such as rural areas, may require higher margins for retailers to earn sufficient income, and that medicines cannot be capped beyond a limit because margins help products reach far-flung areas.

The bench said those justifications were not in favour of patients who pay the higher price. The Solicitor General told the court the government was not averse to the plea, and the bench said its proceedings were intended to strengthen the hands of the government.

What happens next

The court has posted the matter for further hearing on October 27, when the Centre is expected to state its position on the scope of trade-margin regulation. The outcome will determine whether margin control remains a cancer-drug measure or becomes the template for wider regulation of medicines and devices outside scheduled price control.
